why_angle: The cited RV Upgrade Store page lists the 104 V / 132 V cutoff only for the EPO model. No cited page says the cheaper non-EPO Gen II only alerts and does not disconnect, or that both take the same RSM30W surge module. So the roughly $90 extra pays for the shutoff relay and remote cut, not a bigger surge rating. This page lays out that split, with the same-store price gap and Southwire's 102 V cutoff for comparison.

page.title: Smart Plug for an RV: 30 A and 50 A Picks That Cut Shore Power
page.h1: Smart plug for an RV: the 30 A and 50 A units that actually cut power
page.desc: Which RV smart plug disconnects your rig on bad campground voltage, which one only alerts you, and the 15 A plugs that suit appliances inside the RV.
page.answer: Short answer. For RV shore power, use a 30 amp or 50 amp smart surge protector, not a 15 A smart plug. The Hughes Power Watchdog Gen II 30A EPO (PWD30EPOW) cuts power below 104 V or above 132 V and switches remotely by Wi-Fi or Bluetooth; the non-EPO Gen II only alerts.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Auto-shutoff costs about $90 extra. At the same store, 30 A: $279.99 (PWD30EPOW) − $189.95 (PWD30W) = $90.04. 50 A: $338.99 (PWD50EPOW) − $249.99 (PWD50W) = $89.00.
  • A 30 A RV service is 3,600 W: 30 A × 120 V = 3,600 W, the maximum load RV Upgrade Store lists for the PWD30EPOW.
  • A 15 A smart plug carries about half of that: 1,875 W ÷ 3,600 W = 52%. On the Kasa EP40, that 15 A is shared by both outlets.
  • Low-voltage trip point: Hughes EPO trips at 104 V and Southwire Surge Guard 34931 at 102 V. 104 − 102 = 2 V, so the Hughes cuts out slightly earlier in a brownout.

30 A RV; you want it to disconnect by itself and switch it from your phoneHughes PWD30EPOW

Lamp, fan or small dehumidifier inside the RV, no hubKasa EP40
RV that already runs a Z-Wave hub (Hubitat, SmartThings)Minoston MP22Z

Alert-only or auto-shutoff: the part that protects the RV

The Gen II Power Watchdog comes with or without EPO (Emergency Power Off), and both look the same at the pedestal. On a fault, Camping World says the non-EPO PWD30W "turns red and displays the specific error code" and sends a phone alert. Its listing never says it disconnects power. Electric Motor Warehouse says its app can dim or turn off the bay light, and lists no power on/off. The EPO listing is different: "power is immediately cut to your coach when a fault is detected" below 104 V or above 132 V. Power comes back once conditions stay stable for 90 seconds, and you can cut or restore it remotely.

Both 30 A units take the same replaceable surge module. Camping World sells the RSM30W ($39.99) "for use only with the PWD30EPOW, PWD30EPOHW, and PWD30W". So the extra money for EPO pays for the disconnect relay and the remote switch, not more surge capacity (RV Upgrade Store lists 2,300 J for the PWD30EPOW). The disconnect matters if you leave the RV running unattended, because a phone alert does nothing for the A/C compressor while voltage stays low. Mike Sokol (RVelectricity, 12 Oct 2026) describes EMS-type protectors disconnecting above about 128 V or below about 105 V. The EPO models work this way; the PWD30W, by its listing, does not.

On site, the Power Watchdog app connects over Bluetooth with no internet, according to the maker's App Store release notes. Control from away needs the unit joined to a Wi-Fi hotspot. Inside the coach, {buy:kasa-ep40-outdoor-smart-plug} handles single appliances over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi without a hub. If your RV already has a Z-Wave controller, {buy:minoston-mp22z-z-wave-800-outdoor-plug} does the same job on Z-Wave at the same 15 A / 1,875 W rating.

Not recommended

The Gen II 30A PWD30W, if you expect it to protect the RV on its own. It watches and warns, but by its listings it leaves the RV connected while you read the alert. For about $90 more, the PWD30EPOW disconnects on its own. Any household smart plug between the pedestal and the RV: a 15 A plug covers 52% of a 30 A service, and the Kasa EP40 is rated for no more than a 1/2 HP motor.
